claim_traces.claim_text: "Humans only use 10% of their brain capacity — the other 90% remains dormant and untapped."
reasoning_steps: The claim that humans only use 10% of their brain capacity is a well-known scientific myth
Neuroimaging studies, including fMRI and PET scans, show that virtually all parts of the brain have a known function and are active throughout the course of a normal day, even during sleep

Neurologists also note that brain tissue that goes unused typically atrophies or degenerates, and even minor damage to small areas of the brain often results in noticeable cognitive or physical impairments, contradicting the idea that 90% remains dormant
Major neuroscientific and medical institutions universally reject the 10% claim.

reasoning_steps: The claim that the Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye—let alone the only man-made structure visible—is a well-documented myth

According to NASA and reports from astronauts, the Great Wall cannot be seen from low Earth orbit without magnification because it is narrow (typically only about 6 to 9 meters wide) and made of materials that blend into the surrounding landscape
Furthermore, many other man-made structures and features, such as highways, airports, dams, and cities at night, are actually visible from low Earth orbit with the naked eye.

claim_traces.claim_text: "Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short — around 5 feet 2 inches tall."
reasoning_steps: The claim that Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short at around 5 feet 2 inches is a well-known historical misconception
At his autopsy, Napoleon was recorded as measuring 5 feet 2 inches in pre-metric French units (*pieds de roi* and *pouces*)
When converted to modern/British imperial units, this equates to roughly 5 feet 6 inches to 5 feet 7 inches (approximately 168–170 cm)

During the early 19th century, the average height for an adult French male was between 5 feet 2 inches and 5 feet 6 inches, meaning Napoleon was of average or slightly above-average height for his time, rather than unusually short
The myth of his diminutive stature was further popularized by contemporary British propaganda and political caricatures (such as those by James Gillray).
